samples.text:
Today artificial intelligence programs can write essays in a few seconds. Because of this, some people think universities should stop using written assignments that students do at home. I partly agree with this opinion, but I don't think home assignments should be stopped completely.

On the one hand, it is true that AI make cheating very easy. A student can ask a chatbot to write a full essay and then they just change some words and submit it. The teacher cannot always know if the student wrote it or not, so the marks will not show the real ability of students. This is unfair for the honest students who work hard. For this reason, universities should use more exams in the classroom, where students cannot use any technology.

On the other hand, written assignments at home have many benefit. Students have more time to research a topic, read books and think deeply. In an exam, students are under pressure and they only have one or two hours, so they cannot show all of their knowledges. Also, in the real job, people usually write reports with enough time and they can use computers, so home assignments are more similar to the real life.

In my opinion, the best solution is to change the type of assignment. For example, the university can ask students to explain their essay in a short meeting with the teacher, or to write about their own experience which AI does not know. In this way, the assignments will be still useful and cheating will be more difficult.

In conclusion, I partly agree that AI is a big problem for home assignments. However, I believe universities should not stop them totally, but they should change them so that they are more fair.

samples.text:
With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, many students can now produce a well-written essay simply by typing a request into a chatbot. As a result, some argue that universities should stop assessing students through written assignments completed at home. I disagree with this view, as I believe such assignments remain valuable if they are redesigned rather than abandoned.

Admittedly, AI poses a serious challenge to traditional coursework. When a tool can generate a coherent essay in seconds, it becomes difficult for lecturers to know whether the submitted work reflects a student's own understanding. This undermines the fairness of grades and may discourage those who complete their assignments honestly. Supervised exams would obviously reduce this risk, which explain why the idea of abolishing take-home work is attractive to some institutions.

Nevertheless, relying only on timed exams would come at a considerable cost. Extended assignments teach skills that a two-hour exam cannot measure, such as researching independently, evaluating sources and developing an argument over several weeks. These abilities are exactly what graduates need in most professional roles, where reports are rarely written under exam conditions. Removing coursework would therefore make university assessment less relevant to working life.

A more sensible approach is to adapt assignments to the new technology. Universities could require students to submit drafts and notes showing how their ideas developed, or ask them to discuss their work in a short oral examination. Tasks could also be linked to local data, fieldwork or class discussions, which a general AI tool would struggle to reproduce convincingly. Some courses might even permit AI use openly and assess how critically students used it.

In conclusion, while AI has made cheating easier, it does not justify abandoning home-based written assignments. Universities should instead redesign these tasks so they continue to develop and assess the independent thinking that higher education is meant to encourage.

Generative AI has made it possible for almost anyone to produce a fluent essay in seconds, and this has led some commentators to argue that universities should abandon take-home written assignments altogether. I agree with this position only to a limited extent. While unsupervised essays can no longer be trusted as the sole measure of a student's ability, eliminating them entirely would sacrifice some of the most important aims of higher education.

It is undeniable that the traditional take-home essay has become vulnerable. Detection software is unreliable, and a student who submits machine-generated text with a few careful edits may be almost impossible to identify. When grades can be obtained without genuine learning, qualifications lose credibility, and conscientious students are effectively penalised for their honesty. For modules where assessment is heavily weighted towards a single essay, the case for introducing supervised elements is therefore compelling.

However, extended written work serves purposes that invigilated exams cannot. Producing a substantial piece of writing requires students to locate and evaluate sources, sustain an argument and revise their thinking over time. These are precisely the capabilities employers and researchers value, and they cannot be demonstrated in a two-hour sitting where memory and speed are rewarded above reflection. Replacing coursework wholesale with exams would, in effect, narrow what universities teach to what can be tested under pressure.

The more productive response is to rethink how assignments are designed and verified. Requiring annotated drafts, research logs or a brief viva in which students defend their arguments makes outsourcing far less attractive. Tasks grounded in personal fieldwork, recent seminar discussions or original data are also much harder to delegate to a general-purpose model.

In short, AI has exposed genuine weaknesses in take-home assessment, but the appropriate remedy is reform rather than abolition. Universities that adapt their assignments thoughtfully can protect academic integrity without abandoning the independent thinking that written work develops.
